---
title: "Customising the plot"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 150,
  dev = "ragg_png"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(forestmap)
```

This page shows every way you can change a forestmap plot, with an example
of each. All the examples use the `forestmap_example` data that comes with
the package. Most use two study properties to keep the plots small, but
everything works the same with more.

## Headings and order

### Headings

Name each property to set its heading. Without a name, the column name is
used:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Who took part" = "population", "design")
)
```

### Which properties, in which order

The heatmap shows the properties you list, in the order you list them:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Country" = "country", "Population" = "population")
)
```

### Order and names of the rows

Rows follow the order of the factor's levels. Change the order with
`factor(..., levels = ...)`, and rename levels with `labels = ...`:

```{r}
dat <- forestmap_example
dat$population <- factor(
  dat$population,
  levels = c("Clinical", "Children", "Adults"),
  labels = c("Clinical samples", "Children (< 18)", "Adults (18+)")
)

plot_forestmap(
  dat, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design")
)
```

### Numeric properties

A numeric column, such as mean age or sample size, gets a single row in the
heatmap. Each study's tile shows its value, scaled from the lowest value to
the highest. `continuous_style` sets how:

* `"tint"` (the default): the study's colour, pale for low values and full
  strength for high values.
* `"stripe"`: a grey shade for the value, with a band in the study's colour
  along the bottom of the tile.
* `"bar"`: a bar in the study's colour, taller for higher values.

A study with a missing value gets an empty tile.

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Sample size" = "n"),
  continuous_style = "bar"
)
```

`continuous_range` shows the range of values: `"label"` adds it after the
row's name, `"end"` puts a small key at the right end of the row, and
`"legend"` adds a legend below the plot. The default, `"none"`, shows no
range.

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Sample size" = "n"),
  continuous_style = "stripe",
  continuous_range = "legend"
)
```

To show a numeric column as categories instead, one row per value, convert
it with `factor()` first.

The tint and stripe styles show values as shades of grey, so with the
`"greyscale"` palette use `continuous_style = "bar"`.

## Axis titles

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  y_label = "Hedges' g (95% CI)",
  x_label = "Studies, sorted by effect size"
)
```

## Effect size scale

### Ratios: `null_value`

Colours depend on whether each confidence interval excludes the value
meaning "no effect". That's 0 for differences (and log ratios) and 1 for
ratios such as odds ratios. Odds-ratio intervals aren't symmetric, so give
the bounds with `lb` and `ub` rather than a variance. Here the example
effects are converted to odds ratios:

```{r}
odds <- forestmap_example
to_log_or <- pi / sqrt(3)
odds$or <- exp(odds$smd * to_log_or)
odds$or_lower <- exp((odds$smd - 1.96 * sqrt(odds$vi)) * to_log_or)
odds$or_upper <- exp((odds$smd + 1.96 * sqrt(odds$vi)) * to_log_or)

plot_forestmap(
  odds, "or", "or_lower", "or_upper",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  null_value = 1,
  y_label = "Odds ratio (95% CI)"
)
```

Ratios are often easier to read on the log scale: plot `log(or)` with its
variance (`vi`) and the default `null_value = 0`.

### Effects too small to matter: `rope`

`rope` shades a band of effects you consider too small to matter (a
"region of practical equivalence"). Give two numbers, or one number for a
band symmetric around `null_value`:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  rope = c(-0.1, 0.1)
)
```

### Axis range: `y_limits`

By default the y-axis is symmetric around `null_value` and wide enough to
show every confidence interval (for ratios, it starts at 0). Set your own range with `y_limits`; parts of
intervals outside it are cut off:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  y_limits = c(-1, 1.2)
)
```

## Colours

### Built-in palettes

Choose a palette by name. The options are `"default"` (shown in the examples
above), `"okabe_ito"`, `"viridis"` and `"greyscale"`.

`"okabe_ito"` uses blue and vermillion from the Okabe–Ito palette, designed
to stay distinguishable for people with common types of colour blindness:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  palette = "okabe_ito"
)
```

`"viridis"`:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  palette = "viridis"
)
```

`"greyscale"`, for black-and-white printing:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  palette = "greyscale"
)
```

### Your own colours

Give three colours: for positive effects, negative effects, and effects
whose interval includes the null value. Any colour name or hex code works:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  palette = c(positive = "#1b7837", negative = "#762a83", null = "grey75")
)
```

## Font and text size

### Font

`font` takes the name of any font installed on your computer. The default,
`"Roboto Condensed"`, comes with forestmap, so it works everywhere; so do
the generic names `"sans"`, `"serif"` and `"mono"`:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  font = "serif"
)
```

To see which fonts you have, run `systemfonts::system_fonts()$family`. You
can also use a font file that isn't installed, by giving its path:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  font = "fonts/MyFont-Regular.ttf"
)
```

### Text size

`text_size` sets the size of all text, in points (default 9):

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  text_size = 12
)
```

## Panel heights

By default, the heatmap gets more of the plot's height the more rows it has.
`forest_height` sets the forest plot's share of the height yourself, between
0 and 1. Here the forest plot and heatmap get half each:

```{r}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design"),
  forest_height = 0.5
)
```

## Many study properties

With many properties or levels the heatmap gets tall. Two options help.

### Compact layout

`layout = "compact"` puts each property's name beside its rows instead of
on a row of its own:

```{r, fig.height = 5.25}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c(
    "Population" = "population",
    "Outcome measure" = "outcome",
    "Study design" = "design",
    "Country" = "country"
  ),
  layout = "compact"
)
```

### Fewer rows: `max_levels`

`max_levels` sets the most rows any property can have. The most common
levels are kept, and the rest are merged into one "Other" row. With
`max_levels = 3`, the five countries become USA, Australia and Other:

```{r, fig.height = 5.25}
plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c(
    "Population" = "population",
    "Outcome measure" = "outcome",
    "Study design" = "design",
    "Country" = "country"
  ),
  layout = "compact",
  max_levels = 3
)
```

If several levels tie for the last place, all of them are kept and you get a
warning saying so.

## Going further with ggplot2 and patchwork

`plot_forestmap()` returns a [patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaging.com)
of two ggplot2 plots: `p[[1]]` is the forest plot and `p[[2]]` the heatmap.
You can add to either one.

### Title and caption

```{r, fig.height = 5}
p <- plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design")
)

p + patchwork::plot_annotation(
  title = "Effects of the intervention",
  subtitle = "60 studies, sorted by effect size",
  caption = "Simulated data"
)
```

### Show the pooled effect

Add a line to the forest plot, for example at the pooled effect from your
meta-analysis. Here it's a simple inverse-variance (fixed-effect) average:

```{r}
pooled <- weighted.mean(forestmap_example$smd, w = 1 / forestmap_example$vi)

p <- plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design")
)

p[[1]] <- p[[1]] +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = pooled, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text", x = 1, y = pooled, label = "Pooled effect",
    hjust = 0, vjust = -0.6, size = 3, family = "Roboto Condensed"
  )
p
```

Text added with `annotate()` doesn't pick up the plot's font automatically,
so set `family` to the font the plot uses (`"Roboto Condensed"` unless you
chose another).

### Axis breaks

Change where the y-axis labels go with `scale_y_continuous()`. Use round
numbers; `seq()` can create tiny rounding errors that show up as odd labels:

```{r}
p <- plot_forestmap(
  forestmap_example, "smd", vi = "vi",
  moderators = c("Population" = "population", "Study design" = "design")
)

p[[1]] <- p[[1]] + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1))
p
```

## Saving

`plot_forestmap()` doesn't save anything; use `ggplot2::ggsave()` and choose
the size there. The plot looks best at around 7 × 5 inches with four
properties; add height as you add rows.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.png", p, width = 7, height = 5.25, dpi = 300)
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.svg", p, width = 7, height = 5.25)
ggplot2::ggsave("forestmap.pdf", p, width = 7, height = 5.25, device = cairo_pdf)
```

For PDFs, use `device = cairo_pdf`. PDFs (and RStudio's Plots pane) only see
fonts installed on your computer, so install Roboto Condensed (from
`system.file("fonts", package = "forestmap")`) or choose an installed font.
In RStudio you can instead set *Tools > Global Options > General >
Graphics > Backend* to **AGG**.
